units: NZD per share unless stated; net assets in millions
method: LIC NAV per share compounding + exit price-to-NAV discount capitalization at cost of equity (engine route not used -- non-FCF model, hand-built per dcf-methods SKILL.md routing table row 'LIC, investment trust, closed-end fund, VC unit trust'). NOT an FCF DCF.
valuation_philosophy: Barramundi is a closed-end NZX-listed investment company (LIC) externally managed by Fisher Funds, holding a concentrated ~25-35 stock portfolio of Australian-listed equities. It has no revenue in the operating sense, no EBITDA, no capex, no SBC, and zero total debt in every reported period -- a standard FCF/WACC DCF is invalid and is not used, exactly as for the folder's other Fisher Funds-managed sister vehicle MLN.NZ (Marlin Global) and the other LICs AFI.NZ, BIT.NZ and BIF.NZ. This model instead uses the NAV-compounding + exit-discount framework applied consistently across those tickers: (1) start from the most current disclosed NAV per share, not the last audited balance-sheet date, because BRM publishes NAV weekly and the portfolio has moved materially since 31-Dec-2025; (2) project NAV per share forward using a total-return assumption (Australian equity market return net of Fisher Funds' currently severe, demonstrated benchmark underperformance and the 1.25%-stepping-to-0.75%-floor management fee) split between per-share NAV growth and the formulaic 2%-of-average-NAV-per-quarter (~8% p.a.) distribution; (3) apply a scenario exit discount/premium to year-5 NAV, since the market-clearing valuation metric for an LIC is price/NAV, not an earnings multiple; (4) separately value the distribution stream as a 5-year IRR-build cross-check (PV of dividends + PV of year-5 exit value at cost of equity). THE CENTRAL, HONEST FINDING: BRM's plain NAV per share has been essentially FLAT over the eight years to FY2025 ($0.7074 FY2018 -> $0.7063 FY2025, a -0.02% p.a. CAGR) because the fixed ~8% p.a. distribution policy has persistently absorbed almost all of the portfolio's organic total return, exactly the pattern already documented for MLN.NZ under the same Fisher Funds distribution formula -- this is not a modelling assumption, it is the eight-year observed record. FY2026 then broke sharply below even that flat trend: a net loss after tax of $42.9m and an adjusted NAV return of -18.2% against a benchmark that rose +9.2% (one of the worst relative years in the fund's history, following FY2025's own underperformance of +3.9% vs +13.5% and H1 FY2026's -6.6% vs +5.6% -- five consecutive quarters of shortfall), driving NAV per share from $0.7063 (30-Jun-2025) to $0.6328 (31-Dec-2025) to approximately $0.5325 (mid/late-Sept 2026, the most current disclosed marks). The share price discount to NAV has simultaneously widened to 16-21% through September 2026, well beyond the Board's 6% buyback-trigger threshold, and an Aug-2025 warrant tranche (85.2m issued) almost entirely lapsed at the Aug-2026 exercise date rather than convert -- direct market evidence that investors are not willing to commit fresh capital near current NAV levels. The base case in this model assumes Fisher Funds' current severe underperformance moderates somewhat (Board 'extensive engagement' with the Manager, portfolio pivot toward BHP/Rio Tinto and diversification away from the technology names that drove FY2026's loss) but does not fully reverse within the projection horizon, and that the currently extreme 16-21% discount narrows only partially, not to par -- a materially more cautious set of assumptions than were used for BRM's own prior (now-stale) DCF, appropriate given FY2026 was one of the worst years in the fund's history and there is no confirmed evidence yet (no FY2027 annual report exists) that the underperformance has actually turned.

inputs.nav_current_basis_source: Average of the two most recent disclosed weekly NAV prints in the Analysis JSON: $0.5301 (16-Sep-2026) and $0.5348 (23-Sep-2026), rounded to $0.5325. Used in preference to the 31-Dec-2025 audited interim NAV ($0.6328) because the portfolio has declined materially since then (FY2026 full-year adjusted NAV return of -18.2%) and these are the most current disclosed marks as of the valuation date.

This is corrected data: the prior BRM.NZ_DCF.json (2026-08-09) was built before EPS, DPS and shares-outstanding scale corrections were applied to the CSV/core_metrics (EPS/DPS were stored in cents, shares outstanding was a raw count on a millions-denominated row); NAVPerShare itself was not affected by that bug and is unchanged, but per-share EPS/DPS history below reflects the corrected series.

No more recent share count has been published in an extracted filing; the Sept-2026 Analysis JSON notes the Company holds 2.32m shares as treasury stock acquired under the ongoing buyback programme, which is a modest offset not separately netted here because disclosed NAV-per-share prints already reflect shares net of treasury.

inputs.net_debt_treatment_note: Total debt is zero in every reported period -- a genuine, disclosed fact for this unleveraged closed-end equity fund. Cash is already embedded inside NAV per share and is not added again separately; net_debt is set to 0 for schema purposes to avoid double-counting.
inputs.warrants_outcome_note: Only 83,274 of 85,179,108 warrants (0.1%) were exercised at the Aug-2026 expiry -- almost the entire tranche lapsed worthless as the share price/NAV remained well below even the reduced $0.65 strike. This is direct market evidence of weak investor appetite near current NAV levels and is treated as a bearish signal in the scenario narratives, not modelled as a mechanical dilution (since it did not occur).
inputs.distribution_policy: 2% of average NAV distributed per quarter (~8% p.a.), a fixed formula independent of the portfolio's actual total return, in place since Aug-2009
inputs.management_fee_note: 1.25% p.a. of gross asset value, stepping down 0.1pp per 1pp of underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index to a 0.75% floor -- likely at or near the floor through FY2026 given the scale of underperformance
inputs.performance_fee_hurdle: NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index + 7%, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV, subject to a high-water mark; none payable since FY2024
inputs.buyback_trigger_note: Buybacks activated whenever the discount to last-published NAV exceeds 6% (up to 5% of shares on issue per 12-month period). The discount has remained far above threshold through Sept-2026 (16-21%) and the Company continues to accumulate treasury stock, but the widening discount despite active buybacks suggests they have not been sufficient at scale to arrest the trend.
inputs.fx_note: Not applicable -- unlike AFI.NZ or FMG.AX, BRM.NZ's financial statements are reported in NZD and it quotes in NZD on the NZX; no currency conversion is required for this valuation. Portfolio assets are AUD-denominated Australian equities, but this AUD/NZD exposure is a risk factor embedded in NAV volatility (see risks), not a units-conversion issue for the model.
inputs.sbc_note: Not applicable -- Barramundi is an externally-managed investment company; no stock-based compensation or dilution mechanic of that kind exists in this model.
inputs.fcf_dcf_note: Not applicable -- see valuation_philosophy. No FCF projection, WACC-Gordon terminal value, or SBC adjustment is used; schema fields are replaced by the NAV-compounding equivalents below.
inputs.sbc_source: unavailable -- not applicable to an externally-managed LIC; see fcf_dcf_note
inputs.buyback_cash_note: Cash spent on buybacks is not separately quantified for FY2026 in the extracted data (no FY2026 annual report yet extracted); treated as a NAV-per-share-accretive capital-management tool in scenario narratives rather than a projected cash line.

inputs.notes: Model choice: NAV/NTA + exit-discount, per .claude/skills/dcf-methods/SKILL.md routing table row 'LIC, investment trust, closed-end fund, VC unit trust'. This is an UPDATE to the 2026-08-09 BRM.NZ_DCF.json. The prior build is superseded, not silently carried forward, for two reasons: (1) the underlying CSV/core_metrics EPS, DPS and shares-outstanding series have since been corrected for a scale bug (EPS/DPS were stored in cents; shares outstanding was a raw share count on a millions-denominated row) -- no historical per-share DCF driver from the prior file is reused without re-deriving it from the corrected series; (2) FY2026 (year to 30-Jun-2026) has now been reported in full and was one of the worst relative years in the fund's history (-18.2% adjusted NAV return vs +9.2% benchmark), materially below what the prior 2026-08-09 build (built mid-year, before the full FY2026 result) could have anticipated. See the reconciliation block for the explicit bridge from the prior weighted IV to this one.

historical_growth.methodology: Barramundi's own preferred value driver is NAV-per-share TOTAL RETURN (NAV growth + distributions paid), disclosed against a benchmark Australian equity index. Standard revenue/EPS/equity CAGRs are shown for schema completeness but are NOT the growth driver used in projections -- reported NetIncome/EPS is dominated by unrealised/realised mark-to-market portfolio swings (FY2021 +$52.3m vs FY2022 -$34.6m on a broadly similar share count) rather than an operating trend.
historical_growth.growth_rate_source: nav_total_return_base_case_assumption (not a pure historical CAGR -- see notes)
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Revenue/NetIncome/EPS CAGRs are not meaningful for this ticker and are left null rather than computed -- they are dominated by unrealised mark-to-market portfolio swings of the same order of magnitude as net assets. Equity (net assets) CAGR is similarly noisy: it reflects portfolio value swings, warrant proceeds, and DRP/buyback capital-management mix, not organic compounding, and it materially overstates the outlook because it does not reflect the FY2026 decline (equity CAGR windows ending FY2025 predate the -18.2% NAV-return year). Do not use equity CAGR as the growth driver for this ticker.
historical_growth.notes: The defining historical fact for BRM.NZ, exactly mirroring its sister fund MLN.NZ under the same Fisher Funds distribution formula, is that NAV PER SHARE HAS BEEN ESSENTIALLY FLAT over the seven years to FY2025 ($0.7074 FY2018 -> $0.7063 FY2025, a -0.02% p.a. CAGR) because the fixed 2%-of-average-NAV-per-quarter (~8%/yr) distribution policy has persistently absorbed almost all of the portfolio's organic total return. FY2026 then broke sharply below even that flat trend: NAV per share fell a further ~25% in the twelve months to Sept-2026 (from $0.7063 to ~$0.5325), driven by a -18.2% adjusted NAV return against a benchmark that itself rose +9.2% -- a pure stock-selection/manager failure, not a weak Australian market. The base-case 5.5% total-return assumption sits below both BRM's own historical trend and MLN's comparable 7.0% base case, reflecting a materially more cautious read given FY2026 was one of the worst relative years in the fund's history and there is no confirmed evidence yet that the underperformance has reversed (the Board's 'extensive engagement' with the Manager is a stated intention, not a demonstrated outcome).

base.rationale: Australian equity market total return net of Fisher Funds' currently severe, multi-quarter demonstrated underperformance (FY2026: -18.2% vs +9.2% benchmark; FY2025: +3.9% vs +13.5%; H1 FY2026: -6.6% vs +5.6%) only partially moderating -- the Board's 'extensive engagement' with the Manager and the portfolio pivot toward BHP/Rio Tinto are stated intentions, not yet a demonstrated turnaround, so this case assumes performance stabilises closer to but still below the benchmark, not a full reversal. Net of the ~0.75-1.25% fee. The fixed 8%/yr distribution formula then mechanically implies NAV per share continues to DECLINE (-2.5%/yr) at this total-return level, consistent with the accelerating (not merely flat) NAV erosion actually observed through FY2026. Exit discount of 12% sits between the pre-FY2026 historical range (BRM has typically traded at high-single-digit to low-teens discounts) and the extreme 16-21% level reached through Sept-2026, reflecting a view that today's unusually wide discount partially normalises as the FY2026 shock ages, but does not fully close given the warrant tranche's near-total lapse is direct evidence of weak investor appetite even at a reduced strike.

bull.rationale: The Board's escalated engagement with Fisher Funds produces genuine process or portfolio changes (continuing the BHP/Rio Tinto commodity pivot, reducing the technology overweight that drove FY2026's loss) that restore performance to at or above the Australian benchmark within the projection horizon; the fee-floor mechanism keeps costs low while performance recovers; and the discount narrows to the Board's own 6% buyback-trigger threshold as confidence is restored and buybacks are executed at scale.

bear.rationale: Manager underperformance persists structurally (five consecutive quarters of shortfall through FY2026 with no confirmed turnaround; STEEPP process concentration risk shared with sister fund MLN.NZ, which suffered its own severe FY2025 underperformance), the Board-Manager relationship deteriorates further or a disruptive manager/process change itself destroys value in transition, and the discount widens beyond even the current extreme 16-21% level as the warrant tranche's near-total lapse (83,274 of 85.2m exercised) proves to be the leading edge of a broader loss of investor confidence rather than a one-off. A sub-scale, illiquid fund in this position can see its discount become self-reinforcing.

five_year_irr_build_memo.description: Cross-check to the headline 'current NAV x fair discount' intrinsic value: PV of the 5-year dividend stream plus PV of the year-5 exit value (year-5 NAV x scenario exit discount), both discounted at the scenario's cost of equity. This captures compounding of NAV growth (and its decline under the distribution formula) over the horizon that the simpler current-NAV framing does not.

base.terminal_pct_of_value: n/a -- not an FCF DCF; see five_year_irr_build_memo (exit value is ~61% of the 5yr-build fair value)
base.implied_exit_multiple: n/a -- LIC valuation uses P/NAV, not an earnings multiple

entry_price.methodology: Price today such that 5 years of projected base-case dividends plus the year-5 exit value (year-5 NAV x base-case 12% exit discount) discounted at 15% equals that price. Uses base-case cashflows only, per dcf-analyst methodology, with terminal value discounted at the hurdle rate (not at cost of equity).
entry_price.memo: A 15% IRR hurdle applied to an asset whose base-case total return is only ~5.5% p.a., and whose distribution formula is currently mechanically eroding NAV per share, requires buying at a very deep discount to today's NAV (~-36% implied entry P/NAV, i.e. NZ$0.3404 against the current $0.5325 NAV). This is a plausible target only if the market's current 16-21% discount widens further before any recovery -- a real possibility given the warrant tranche's near-total lapse already signals weak investor appetite at these levels, but not a near-certainty. A more realistic read is to judge BRM against its ~10% cost of equity rather than a private-equity-style 15% hurdle: today's actual price (NZ$0.45, a ~15.5% discount to the current $0.5325 NAV) already sits inside the base-case assumed 12% fair-discount range, meaning the current price offers a prospective return close to but modestly below the base-case ~5.5% total return, once the wider entry discount is factored in.

sanity_check.basis: SBC-adjusted on both sides (EPS less SBC/share; EBITDA less SBC), so these deliberately do not match GAAP screener multiples.

sensitivity.methodology: 5-year IRR-build fair value (PV of dividends + PV of exit value at year-5 NAV x row exit discount, both discounted at the 10.0% base-case cost of equity) in NZD.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Not the house 25/50/25 LIC default: bear is overweighted to 30% (from base) and bull trimmed to 20% because BRM.NZ, unlike MLN.NZ or AFI.NZ at the time of their builds, is coming off a confirmed, severe, five-consecutive-quarter underperformance record with an active Board-Manager governance escalation and no confirmed evidence yet of a turnaround -- the downside case (persistent underperformance, further discount widening) is better evidenced in the current record than the upside case (a Manager turnaround that has been announced as an intention but not yet demonstrated in results).
